lines: One of the four simultaneous Kiss solo albums, it was produced by Eddie Kramer and Ace Frehley with Anton Fig on drums. "New York Groove", a cover of the 1975 Hello single, became the biggest hit from any of the four solo records.

Recorded across four shows in May through July 1975 and overdubbed at Electric Lady Studios, it was the breakthrough record that rescued both Kiss and Casablanca Records. It captured on vinyl the live intensity that the first three studio albums had only hinted at.

Recorded primarily at the Forum in Los Angeles in August 1977, with two tracks from Budokan in April. Side four consists of new studio songs recorded at Capitol Theatre in Passaic, New Jersey in September, with Bob Kulick on lead guitar.

Recorded over three nights on the Revenge tour, it was the first Kiss live album made by a non-original lineup. The set mixes classics with newer material and captures the Stanley-Simmons-Kulick-Singer era at its peak.
Produced by Paul Stanley. The only Kiss studio album to feature Mark St. John. Mark also played two and a half concerts with Kiss. Includes the mega-hit "Heaven's On Fire".

The first Kiss album to officially feature Bruce Kulick as lead guitarist after he finished the previous tour in Mark St. John's place. Produced by Paul Stanley and Gene Simmons in New York, it leaned hard into mid-1980s glam metal and MTV styling, with "Tears Are Falling" as the standout single.

Recorded in 1995 and 1996, it was shelved once the original-lineup reunion took priority and then leaked widely before official release. Its dark, grunge-tinged sound makes it the most stylistically unusual album in the Kiss catalog, and it was the last studio album with Bruce Kulick.
Produced by Ron Nevison, its slick, keyboard-heavy sound aimed squarely at the late-1980s arena-rock market, and "Crazy Crazy Nights" became a major hit in the UK.

Produced by Michael James Jackson with Paul Stanley and Gene Simmons, it was Kiss' heaviest studio album to date and a deliberate reaction against the pop lean of the previous records. Ace Frehley appeared on the cover but did not play on the album. Vinnie Vincent handled the lead guitar parts.

Produced by Bob Ezrin, it marked a major expansion of the Kiss sound with orchestration, a children's choir, spoken effects, and more elaborate arrangements. "Beth", sung by Peter Criss, became the breakout crossover hit that pushed the band into the mainstream. Ken Kelly's drawing is the most iconic of all Kiss album covers.
Kiss' first greatest-hits set remixed or edited many familiar tracks instead of simply compiling the original album versions. "Strutter" was newly re-recorded with a disco pulse as "Strutter '78".

Recorded in just 10 days at Electric Lady Studios, it was co-produced by Casablanca president Neil Bogart. "Rock And Roll All Nite" became the band's signature song after "Alive!". The image of the band dressed in suits and ties on the front cover was another visual success.

Produced by Vini Poncia, it took Kiss further into disco and pop, with "I Was Made For Lovin' You" becoming one of the band's biggest international hits. Peter Criss, sidelined by injury and personal issues, played drums only on "Dirty Livin'", while Anton Fig played on the rest of the album.

One of the four simultaneous Kiss solo albums, it was produced by Gene Simmons and Sean Delaney and loaded with outside guests including Joe Perry, Bob Seger, Rick Nielsen, Donna Summer, Cher, and Katey Sagal. Although Simmons was Kiss' bassist, Neil Jason handled most of the bass while Simmons played mainly guitar.

Issued to support the Alive/Worldwide reunion era, the US edition focuses on hits from 1974 to 1980 and adds an exclusive live "Shout It Out Loud" from Tiger Stadium in Detroit. Non-US pressings expanded the track list with "God Gave Rock 'N Roll To You" and other songs.

Recorded at The Village in Los Angeles, it was the band's first recording made outside New York and again produced by Kenny Kerner and Richie Wise. Introduced staples including "Parasite", "Watchin' You", and "Got To Choose". The visual flirtation with Japanese culture would serve the band very well.

Produced by Gene Simmons and Paul Stanley at the Fortress in Hollywood, it has 15 tracks, more than any other Kiss studio album. "Forever", co-written with Michael Bolton, became one of the band's biggest late-era hits, and the album was the final full studio release to feature Eric Carr.

Assembled for markets outside the United States after The Elder underperformed, it mixed older material with four new studio tracks produced by Michael James Jackson. Ace Frehley appeared on the sleeve but did not play on the new songs. Instead, Bob Kulick again handled the lead guitar.

Recorded in November 1973 at Bell Sound Studios in New York City in just 13 days, many of the songs on the band's self-titled debut album are classics to this day. Produced by Kenny Kerner and Richie Wise.

Kiss' first album without makeup, and their first for Mercury Records, making it a clean break from the masked era. Vinnie Vincent co-wrote much of the material, and was now an official member of the band. The title track became a centerpiece of the band's 1980s comeback.

Produced by Kiss and Eddie Kramer at the Record Plant, it was the first Kiss album to feature lead vocals from all four members. "Shock Me" gave Ace Frehley his first lead vocal on a Kiss album, inspired by the onstage electrocution incident that had nearly killed him.

Produced by Paul Stanley and Greg Collins, it was Kiss' final studio album and was recorded with the same Stanley-Simmons-Thayer-Singer lineup as Sonic Boom. A stripped-down, back-to-basics hard-rock record with almost no outside songwriters.

One of the four simultaneous Kiss solo albums, it was produced by Paul Stanley and Jeff Glixman and is the only one made entirely of original songs. Bob Kulick handled the lead guitar throughout, while Stanley pursued the most polished and overtly Kiss-like of the four albums.

One of the four simultaneous Kiss solo albums, it was produced by Vini Poncia, who later produced Dynasty and Unmasked for Kiss. Drawing on Criss's Motown and R&B influences, it reworked material from his pre-Kiss band Lips and moved furthest away from the band's hard-rock identity.

Produced by Bruce Fairbairn, it was marketed as the original lineup's studio reunion, but most of the album was actually built with uncredited session players. Peter Criss played drums only on "Into The Void", and Ace Frehley performed on just two tracks.

Produced by Bob Ezrin, it was the band's first album with him since "The Elder" and their first studio release with drummer Eric Singer. Dedicated to Eric Carr, it closes with "Carr Jam 1981", built from a guitar-and-drum instrumental he had recorded years earlier. Features the stand-out hit "God Gave Rock 'N Roll To You".

Recorded at the Star Theatre in Nanuet with the Record Plant mobile truck, it was a back-to-basics reaction to the studio complexity of Destroyer. It yielded two of the band's most durable songs, "Hard Luck Woman" and "Calling Dr. Love".

Kiss' second US hits compilation added two new songs, "Let's Put The X In Sex" and "(You Make Me) Rock Hard", both co-written with Desmond Child and produced by Paul Stanley. Eric Carr also re-recorded "Beth" with his own lead vocal, his first on a Kiss album.
Produced by Paul Stanley and Greg Collins, it was Kiss' first studio album in eleven years and the first with Tommy Thayer and Eric Singer as full recording members.

Recorded in Melbourne with the 60-piece Melbourne Symphony Orchestra, whose members appeared in Kiss makeup and tuxedos. It was the first Kiss live album with Tommy Thayer as the "Spaceman" and the last to feature Peter Criss.
Produced by Bob Ezrin, it was a concept album built around a script for a movie that did not happen. It was the first album with Eric Carr, and the last to feature Ace Frehley as an active member.

Produced by Vini Poncia, it pushed the band even further into glossy pop. Peter Criss was credited but did not play on the record. Anton Fig handled all the drum tracks. Peter did sing "Dirty Livin'".

Recorded for MTV Unplugged at Sony Music Studios, it became the only public performance where the original four members appeared together without makeup. Ace Frehley and Peter Criss joined the current lineup for the final songs, and the fan response directly triggered the reunion tour.

Built to support the reunion era, it pulls mostly from Alive! and Alive II and includes four tracks presented as previously unreleased outtakes that were actually new studio re-recordings. It closes with a 17-minute group interview conducted by Jay Leno.
